lines.text: There are many named kinds. A stepped tenon, the jūhozo, or stacked tenon, for example, goes at the top of a post where a wall plate and a beam stack up. This episode looks at the joint where a post meets a sill.

lines.text: For posts outside the bearing walls, the Flat 35 house specification lists two families of options. A short tenon, held with a metal plate, bracket or staple. Or a long tenon, pinned with a komisen.

lines.text: How big is a short tenon? The test standard for Japan's certified joint hardware uses one on a hundred-and-five millimeter post and sill: thirty thick, eighty-five wide, fifty deep.

lines.text: In a bearing wall, Japan's standard detail drawings give a plain short tenon a joint rating of zero: it isn't counted on to stop the post pulling out. That job needs rated hardware, or a pinned long tenon.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: The long tenon goes deep into the sill. A hardwood pin, the komisen, is driven sideways through sill and tenon together. Where a tenon passes right through and sticks out, it can instead be pinned through that projecting part: a hanasen.

lines.tts: The long tenon goes deep into the sill. A hardwood pin, the koh-mee-sen, is driven sideways through sill and tenon together. Where a tenon passes right through and sticks out, it can instead be pinned through that projecting part: a hah-nah-sen.

lines.text: The holes are made so the pin draws the two members together: the hole through the tenon is bored slightly closer to the shoulder than the hole through the sill. Driving the pin pulls the post down tight onto the sill.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: The public-works specification asks for square holes and pins; one lab report notes round pins are now more common. In a bearing wall, the Flat 35 specification puts a pinned long tenon in the same class as an L-shaped metal corner plate.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Cutting the tenon: rip down the cheeks first, then crosscut the shoulder, with the kerf on the waste side of its line. The public-works specification warns: don't saw the crosscuts too deep.

lines.text: In the skills-test manual's practice piece, a beam's tenon is cut a little loose in thickness and a little tight in width, as we saw in Episode 4.

lines.text: Chopping the mortise: use a mortise chisel a little narrower than the hole. Start a few millimeters inside the lines, rough it out, then pare back to the lines and check the depth.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: The manual adds: strike lightly when the edge runs along the grain, and a little harder when it cuts across it.

lines.text: Fit it in small steps. In the manual's practice piece, the width goes in with light taps over a block of wood; the thickness, by hand. For posts, the public-works specification asks for a snug fit: driven in, and fully seated.

lines.text: A short tenon needs hardware to hold. A long tenon can be pinned so it pulls itself tight. And a snug fit, made in small steps, does the rest.

lines.text: One note: sharp-tool technique, and how to use these tools safely, is best learned from a teacher, at a bench, in person.
